source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) Generative Language Modeling for Automated Theorem Proving (GPT-f)
finding: A transformer prover for Metamath closed more held-out proofs than the prior system. Its short proofs were accepted into the main Metamath library, the first time a deep-learning system contributed proofs a formal community adopted.
numbers: 56.22% of held-out test proofs closed vs 21.16% for the current Metamath prover baseline.
limits: Metamath only; proofs are short (about 10-20 steps) and the kernel is tiny, so results do not transfer directly to Lean or Isabelle.
agent_relevance: The kernel is the judge: an untrusted generator plus a trusted checker gives real gains and accepted contributions. Core of S8 VERIFY.

source: Han, Rute, Wu, Ayers, Polu (2021) PACT: Proof Artifact Co-training for Theorem Proving with Language Models
finding: Training the tactic model on auxiliary tasks mined from proof terms (co-training) raised Lean (mathlib) proving rates. Web math pre-training also helped.
numbers: Held-out theorem pass rate rose from 32% to 48.4%; refl baseline about 10-11.6%, tidy-bfs about 22-32%; best model 37.1% (1043 proofs) on a newer split vs tidy-bfs 21.8% and refl 11.6%.
limits: Gains come from training, not from a scaffold. mathlib snapshot of 2021; leakage with pretraining not fully ruled out.
agent_relevance: Symbolic baselines (tidy, refl) are strong floors; an agent should call cheap automation first and keep the LLM for the rest.

source: Zheng, Han, Polu (2021) miniF2F: a cross-system benchmark for formal Olympiad-level mathematics
finding: Benchmark of 488 Olympiad-level problems formalized across Lean, Metamath, Isabelle and HOL Light. GPT-f style tactic models in Lean gave the first reported scores.
numbers: Lean GPT-f baseline: Pass@1 24.6% and Pass@8 29.2% on miniF2F-test (a weaker Lean model: Pass@1 1.3%, Pass@8 1.6%).
limits: Statements were hand-formalized; later work found formalization mismatches. Scores are not comparable across systems with different statement versions.
agent_relevance: A fixed benchmark with a kernel check allows exact measurement of any scaffold change on the agent.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Thor: Wielding Hammers to Integrate Language Models and Automated Theorem Provers
finding: Let the LM write proof steps and call a hammer (Sledgehammer) for premise selection when unsure. The combined system beats either alone.
numbers: PISA: LM alone 39.0% to Thor 57.0%; 8.2% of problems solved by neither LM nor Sledgehammer alone. miniF2F-test: 29.9% vs 29.6% for the expert-iteration baseline with much less compute.
limits: Needs a hammer-enabled prover (Isabelle). Hammer timeouts matter.
agent_relevance: Template for tool delegation: the model decides when to hand a subgoal to a symbolic solver.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove: Guiding Formal Theorem Provers with Informal Proofs
finding: Draft an informal proof with an LLM, turn it into a formal sketch with holes, then close holes with automation. Informal proofs lift Isabelle results a lot.
numbers: miniF2F-valid 42.6% and test 39.3% with human informal proofs (test 38.9% with model drafts); abstract: 20.9% to 39.3%. Sledgehammer 9.9% valid / 20.9% test; Sledgehammer+heuristics 18.0% / 35.2%; bigger Minerva drafts did not help (540B: 30.3% test).
limits: Drafts must be mostly right; larger drafting model did not monotonically help. Heuristics baseline already 35.2% on test.
agent_relevance: Supports plan then formalize: an outline with open gaps, then verify each gap separately.

source: Lample et al. (2022) HyperTree Proof Search for Neural Theorem Proving
finding: Hypertree search over proof goals with online training raised Metamath and Lean scores.
numbers: Metamath held-out 65.4% (vs 56.5% GPT-f), 82.6% with online training on unproved theorems; miniF2F-curriculum 31% to 42%; miniF2F-valid 58.6% (with training) and test 41.0% in later comparison tables.
limits: Large compute; online training on test-like theorems can inflate numbers.
agent_relevance: Search structure over subgoals matters; supports tree-style exploration with kernel-verified leaves.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
finding: Open Lean benchmark and ReProver, a retrieval-augmented tactic generator. Premise retrieval helped; zero-shot GPT-4 was weak.
numbers: Pass@1 random split: ReProver 51.2%, no retrieval 47.6%, GPT-4 29.0%, tidy 23.8%. novel_premises split: ReProver 26.3%, no retrieval 23.2%, GPT-4 7.4%, tidy 5.3%. Retriever R@10: 38.4 vs BM25 17.2 (random).
limits: Random split rewards memorization; novel_premises is much harder. GPT-4 data contamination possible (proofs on GitHub before its cutoff).
agent_relevance: Test whether an agent generalizes to new lemmas, not just recalls them. Use the harder split for any claim.

source: Welleck & Saha (2023) LLMSTEP: LLM proofstep suggestions in Lean
finding: A Lean 4 tactic that sends the proof state to a server and returns language-model tactic suggestions inside the editor. Human stays in the loop.
numbers: Paper reports it outperforms recent open-source tactic-prediction models on a standard task; no user-study numbers.
limits: Tool paper; no controlled study of human productivity.
agent_relevance: Human-in-the-loop pattern: model suggests, kernel filters, person chooses.

source: Song, Yang, Anandkumar (2024) Towards Large Language Models as Copilots for Theorem Proving in Lean (Lean Copilot)
finding: LLM steps inside Lean: suggest tactics, search whole proofs, or select premises, compared with rule-based AESOP.
numbers: Manual tactics needed per theorem: 2.08 (suggest) vs 3.86 (AESOP). Proof steps automated: AESOP 40.1%, SUGGEST_TACTICS 58.4%, SEARCH_PROOF 74.2%.
limits: Small test set of textbook theorems; one task set.
agent_relevance: Hybrid beats either: combine rule-based automation with LLM suggestion and check every step.

source: Thakur et al. (2024) An In-Context Learning Agent for Formal Theorem-Proving (COPRA)
finding: GPT-4 in a stateful backtracking loop that runs tactics, reads errors, and gets retrieved lemmas. Each part adds measurable gain.
numbers: miniF2F-test pass@1: few-shot GPT-4 13.52%; COPRA 26.63% (60 queries); no backtracking 24.59%; +retrieval 29.09%; +retrieval+informal 29.92% (100 queries: 30.74%); ReProver 25.00%; COPRA with GPT-3.5 9.02%, CodeLlama 5.73%; few-shot GPT-3.5 2.8%.
limits: Closed model, cost. Gains over ReProver are small. Weaker models gain little.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue to our loop: propose, execute in checker, feed error back, backtrack. Backtracking is worth about 2 points; retrieval about 2.5.

source: Lu, Delaware, Zhang (2024) Proof Automation with Large Language Models (PALM)
finding: Formative study of 520 GPT-3.5 Coq proof errors: it gets the high-level plan right and low-level details wrong. PALM generates, then repairs with symbolic methods.
numbers: Error mix: wrong theorem application 49.6%, invalid reference 15.2%, incorrect rewrite 11.7%, redundant intros 10.8%, tactic misuse 8.5%, bullet misuse 3.7%. Over about 10.8K theorems: Passport 14.4%, Proverbot9001 17.1%, DSP 22.9%, one-shot GPT-3.5 3.7%, GPT-4o 6.4%; PALM proves 76.6-180.4% more; 1270 theorems beyond other approaches.
limits: Coq only; repair depends on the error classes seen.
agent_relevance: Repair step should target the common low-level errors, not regenerate the whole plan.

source: Kasibatla et al. (2024) Cobblestone: Divide-and-Conquer Approach for Automating Formal Verification
finding: Use partial LLM proofs to split goals, keep the verified parts, and retry only the rest. Result stays sound because Coq checks everything.
numbers: 48% of CoqGym100 theorems and 38% on another set; Proverbot9001 and CoqHammer 30% and 27%; CoT and plain prompting 25% and 19%; with oracle structure up to 58%; about $1.25 and 14.7 minutes per run; non-LLM tools prove 14 theorems Cobblestone cannot.
limits: Controls for leakage on 4 Coq benchmarks; Coq only.
agent_relevance: Keep verified sub-results and retry only failed parts: support for incremental verification (S8).

source: Thompson et al. (2024) Rango: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Proving for Automated Software Verification
finding: Fine-tuned Coq prover that retrieves similar proofs and lemmas from the current project. Adding relevant proofs to context is the biggest lever.
numbers: Proves 32.0% (3,325) of theorems, 29% more than Tactician, 66% more than Proverbot9001; adding retrieved proofs gives a 47% relative increase.
limits: Single benchmark; retrieved proofs may overlap training data.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of worked examples from the same project beats a bare prompt.

source: Tsoukalas et al. (2024) PutnamBench
finding: Hard college-competition benchmark in Lean 4, Isabelle, Coq. Early LLM provers nearly all failed.
numbers: 640 problems Lean/Isabelle, 412 Coq. Lean: GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, ReProver 0 of 640. Isabelle: DSP 4, Sledgehammer 3, GPT-4 1 of 640. Coq: GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, Tactician 0, CoqHammer 0 of 412.
limits: 2024 numbers; later systems went far higher.
agent_relevance: Shows how fast the field moved: near zero in 2024, hundreds in 2025. Use as an anti-ceiling check.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover: Advancing Theorem Proving in LLMs through Large-Scale Synthetic Data
finding: Autoformalize about 8 million statements, filter, and train by expert iteration; whole-proof generation beats GPT-4.
numbers: miniF2F-test whole-proof 46.3% with 64 samples (52% cumulative) vs GPT-4 23.0% and tree-search RL 41.0%; FIMO 4 of 148 solved with 100 samples (5 with 4096) vs 0 for GPT-4; at least 20% of autoformalized statements were flawed.
limits: Synthetic statements are noisy; filtering matters.
agent_relevance: Statement correctness is a risk: check that the verified statement means what was asked.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Selene: Pioneering Automated Proof in Software Verification
finding: Benchmark of 360 lemmas from the seL4 Isabelle proof. Harder lemmas break GPT-4; retrieval, dependency and error-fix augmentations help.
numbers: GPT-4 ACC#1: P1 (one-line proofs) 41.7%, P2 7.7%, P3 0%, definitions 10.5%; ACC#5 on P1 51.8%. With similar-lemma retrieval P1 47.5%, dependency 52.5%, fixing 53.2%, try-again 49.6%; similar+fixing P1 61.9%, P2 20.2%. Over half of errors were unfinished goals.
limits: sorry and oops counted as failures because they bypass the kernel. One real project.
agent_relevance: Real-project difficulty is far above contest benchmarks. Ban sorry-style escapes in any verifier loop.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover
finding: Open prover trained on 1.64 million autoformalized statements with iterative expert iteration.
numbers: 57.6% Pass@32 on miniF2F; over 60% after further iteration.
limits: Single-sample figures much lower.
agent_relevance: More samples with a free verifier is a cheap scaling axis.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Kimina-Prover Preview
finding: RL-trained reasoning prover that writes informal thinking before the Lean proof, with verifier reward.
numbers: miniF2F-test 80.7% at pass@8192; 7B model 63.1% at pass@32 and 70.8% at pass@1024; distilled 72B 52.5% at pass@1.
limits: Needs RL with verifier reward and large sample counts.
agent_relevance: Thinking before formalizing fits plan-then-check; the training signal is the kernel.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2
finding: Recursive subgoal decomposition by a general LLM, then a prover closes subgoals; cold-start data for RL with long chain of thought.
numbers: miniF2F-test 88.9% at Pass@8192 (671B); CoT 7B 68.85% at 32 and 77.87% at 1024; non-CoT 671B Pass@1 52.94%; ProofNet-test 37.1% at Pass@1024; PutnamBench 47 of 658; ProverBench AIME 217/244.
limits: Huge compute; Putnam still under 8%.
agent_relevance: Decompose into lemmas then fill: matches an outline with gap-by-gap verification.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Seed-Prover: Deep and Broad Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving
finding: Whole-proof model that refines proofs from Lean feedback, proved lemmas and its own summaries, with light, medium, heavy test-time settings.
numbers: IMO 2025: 4 of 6 within the contest, 5 of 6 afterwards; past IMO 78.1%; miniF2F-test 99.6%, valid 100%; PutnamBench 331/657 vs prior best 86/657; CombiBench 30.0% vs 10.0%; MiniCTX-v2 81.8% vs 44.3%.
limits: Closed model, very large inference budgets; one test problem failed even under heavy.
agent_relevance: Iterating on compiler feedback beats independent Pass@k sampling, per the authors; key design for a verify-refine loop.

source: Varambally et al. (2026) Hilbert: Recursively Building Formal Proofs with Informal Reasoning
finding: Agent loop: informal reasoner (Gemini) plans, prover LLM does Lean tactics, verifier checks, retriever finds theorems; recursive decomposition on failure.
numbers: miniF2F 99.2% (6.6 points above best public method); PutnamBench 462/660 (70.0%) vs Seed-Prover 50.4%, a 422% gain over best public baseline; Gemini 2.5 Pro alone 49.1% on miniF2F at 16,384 attempts; best open provers about 13% on Putnam vs about 83% for informal reasoning.
limits: Depends on a strong closed reasoner; costs not fully comparable.
agent_relevance: General reasoner plus small prover plus kernel is a scaffold, not training: our setting. Scaffolding closes most of the gap.

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet: Autoformalizing and Formally Proving Undergraduate-Level Mathematics
finding: 371 undergraduate problems with formal statements and informal proofs in Lean 3 for autoformalization and proving.
numbers: Benchmark paper with low initial scores; later DeepSeek-Prover-V2 reports 37.1% at Pass@1024 on ProofNet-test.
limits: Lean 3 original; Lean 4 translation used later.
agent_relevance: Undergraduate level exposes the gap between competition tricks and library use.

source: Yang & Deng (2019) CoqGym (as cited in miniF2F)
finding: Early neural Coq prover; the miniF2F text cites its held-out result.
numbers: 30.0% held-out pass rate (cited, not read in the original).
limits: Not opened; figure from a citing paper.
agent_relevance: Baseline for neural versus symbolic comparison in Coq.

source: Sanchez-Stern et al. (2020) Proverbot9001 (as cited in Cobblestone and Rango)
finding: Learned predictor plus search for Coq proofs; non-LLM baseline in later LLM papers.
numbers: Cited: 19.8% on CoqGym (from Cobblestone text); Rango beats it by 66%.
limits: Not opened; numbers from citing papers.
agent_relevance: Classical learned provers remain competitive floors.

source: Cross-paper pattern: verifier feedback vs independent sampling (Seed-Prover, COPRA, Cobblestone, Selene)
finding: Across the opened papers, systems that feed kernel or compiler errors back, keep verified lemmas, and retry only failed parts beat blind Pass@k sampling.
numbers: COPRA: backtracking +2.0 points (24.59 to 26.63); Selene fixing +11.5 points on P1 (41.7 to 53.2); Cobblestone 48% vs 25% (CoT) and 19% (plain); Seed-Prover: iterative refinement beats Pass@k.
limits: Different benchmarks and models; effects not additive. Synthesis by this agent.
agent_relevance: S8 VERIFY should be a loop over checkable sub-claims with error text returned, never a final yes/no.

source: Cross-paper pattern: the checker's escape hatches (Selene, DeepSeek-Prover, LeanDojo)
finding: Kernel acceptance only means the stated theorem was proved. sorry/oops, wrong autoformalization and leakage can fake or inflate success.
numbers: Selene counts sorry/oops/timeouts as failure; DeepSeek-Prover found at least 20% of autoformalized statements flawed; LeanDojo flags GPT-4 contamination.
limits: Synthesis by this agent.
agent_relevance: Verify the statement as well as the proof; exclude escape tokens; test on novel-premise splits.
